claim: Wnt proteins regulate development and adult tissue homeostasis by binding and activating cell-surface Frizzled receptors and co-receptors including LRP5/6.
source: Secreted Wnt proteins regulate development and adult tissue homeostasis by binding and activating cell-surface Frizzled receptors and co-receptors including LRP5/6.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Wnt signaling pathways.

claim: The hydrophobicity of Wnt proteins has complicated their purification and limited their use in basic research and as therapeutics.
source: The hydrophobicity of Wnt proteins has complicated their purification and limited their use in basic research and as therapeutics.
evidence: This is a known challenge in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Modular tetravalent antibodies can recruit Frizzled and LRP5/6 in a manner that phenocopies the activities of Wnts both in vitro and in vivo.
source: We describe modular tetravalent antibodies that can recruit Frizzled and LRP5/6 in a manner that phenocopies the activities of Wnts both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: FLAgs can be engineered with specificity for one, two or multiple members of the Frizzled family.
source: The modular nature of these synthetic Frizzled and LRP5/6 Agonists, called FLAgs, enables tailored engineering of specificity for one, two or multiple members of the Frizzled family.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the construction and testing of various FLAg variants with different specificities.

claim: FLAgs underlie differentiation of pluripotent stem cells.
source: We show that FLAgs underlie differentiation of pluripotent stem cells, sustain organoid growth, and activate stem cells in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing mesoderm differentiation in hPSCs treated with FLAgs.

claim: FLAgs sustain organoid growth.
source: We show that FLAgs underlie differentiation of pluripotent stem cells, sustain organoid growth, and activate stem cells in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing FLAgs can rescue organoid growth in the presence of Wnt inhibitors.

claim: FLAgs activate stem cells in vivo.
source: We show that FLAgs underlie differentiation of pluripotent stem cells, sustain organoid growth, and activate stem cells in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo mouse experiments showing rescue of LGR5+ intestinal stem cells.

claim: In humans, 19 Wnt proteins interact with a receptor complex composed of one of ten Frizzled (FZD) receptors and one of several co-receptors.
source: In humans, 19 Wnt proteins interact with a receptor complex composed of one of ten Frizzled (FZD) receptors and one of several co-receptors that guide the selective engagement of different intracellular signaling branches (Angers and Moon, 2009; Wodarz and Nusse, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wnt interacts with a FZD and a single transmembrane LRP5 or LRP6 co-receptor to stabilize intracellular βcatenin and regulate genes involved in tissue stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: In the best characterized pathway, Wnt interacts with a FZD and a single transmembrane LRP5 or LRP6 co-receptor to stabilize intracellular βcatenin and regulate genes involved in tissue stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This describes the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway, which is established knowledge.

claim: Wnt binds to the cysteine rich domain (CRD) of FZD.
source: Wnt binds to the cysteine rich domain (CRD) of FZD (Janda et al., 2012) and to either the first two or last two propeller domains of LRP5/6 (Bourhis et al., 2010), and these interactions are thought to allosterically modulate the FZD seven-transmembrane domain to enable recruitment of Disheveled and allow phosphorylation of the LRP5/6 intracellular domain (Davidson et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janda et al., 2012.

claim: Wnt binds to either the first two or last two propeller domains of LRP5/6.
source: Wnt binds to the cysteine rich domain (CRD) of FZD (Janda et al., 2012) and to either the first two or last two propeller domains of LRP5/6 (Bourhis et al., 2010), and these interactions are thought to allosterically modulate the FZD seven-transmembrane domain to enable recruitment of Disheveled and allow phosphorylation of the LRP5/6 intracellular domain (Davidson et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bourhis et al., 2010.

claim: Wnt-FZD-LRP interactions are thought to allosterically modulate the FZD seven-transmembrane domain to enable recruitment of Disheveled and allow phosphorylation of the LRP5/6 intracellular domain.
source: Wnt binds to the cysteine rich domain (CRD) of FZD (Janda et al., 2012) and to either the first two or last two propeller domains of LRP5/6 (Bourhis et al., 2010), and these interactions are thought to allosterically modulate the FZD seven-transmembrane domain to enable recruitment of Disheveled and allow phosphorylation of the LRP5/6 intracellular domain (Davidson et al., 2005; Zeng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2005 and Zeng et al., 2005.

claim: Wnts require lipidation for function.
source: Wnts require lipidation for function (Janda et al., 2012; Kadowaki et al., 1996) and their hydrophobic nature complicates biochemical manipulation; consequently, only a few Wnts have been purified (Willert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janda et al., 2012 and Kadowaki et al., 1996.

claim: Only a few Wnts have been purified.
source: Wnts require lipidation for function (Janda et al., 2012; Kadowaki et al., 1996) and their hydrophobic nature complicates biochemical manipulation; consequently, only a few Wnts have been purified (Willert et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Willert et al., 2003.

claim: Wnts are inherently cross-reactive for multiple receptors, especially when overexpressed or applied at high dose.
source: Furthermore, Wnts are inherently cross-reactive for multiple receptors, especially when overexpressed or applied at high dose (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; He et al., 1997; Holmen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; He et al., 1997; and Holmen et al., 2002.

claim: It has been impossible to activate Frizzled receptor complexes selectively to determine the specific functions of each in different contexts.
source: As a result, it has been impossible to activate Frizzled receptor complexes selectively to determine the specific functions of each in different contexts or to evaluate their therapeutic potential for degenerative conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current tools in the field.

claim: Bivalent Wnt surrogates have been developed by fusing an LRP5/6-binding fragment from the natural protein DKK1 to an engineered ligand for FZD CRDs.
source: Recently, bivalent Wnt surrogates have been developed by fusing an LRP5/6-binding fragment from the natural protein DKK1 to an engineered ligand for FZD CRDs (Janda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janda et al., 2017.

claim: Bivalent Wnt surrogates activated βcatenin signaling in vitro and in vivo when delivered using adenovirus.
source: These Wnt surrogates activated βcatenin signaling in vitro and in vivo when delivered using adenovirus.
evidence: This refers to the work by Janda et al., 2017.

claim: FLAgs are composed of human antibody domains.
source: FLAgs are composed of human antibody domains, and consequently, they are highly stable, amenable to large-scale production and facile purification, have predictable pharmacokinetics, and are likely to exhibit low immunogenicity.
evidence: This is a design feature of the FLAgs described in the manuscript.

claim: FLAgs are highly stable, amenable to large-scale production and facile purification, have predictable pharmacokinetics, and are likely to exhibit low immunogenicity.
source: FLAgs are composed of human antibody domains, and consequently, they are highly stable, amenable to large-scale production and facile purification, have predictable pharmacokinetics, and are likely to exhibit low immunogenicity.
evidence: These are inferred properties based on the human antibody composition and general knowledge of antibody properties.

claim: A pan-FZD Ab (FP) recognized FZD1/2/4/5/7/8.
source: Systematic characterization revealed a continuum of specificity profiles with some Abs displaying broad specificities, exemplified by a pan-FZD Ab (FP) that recognized FZD1/2/4/5/7/8 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), others displaying more restricted specificities, and some being monospecific.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Two Abs (L61 and L63) that targeted the extracellular domain (ECD) of human LRP6 bound to non-overlapping epitopes.
source: We also developed two Abs that targeted the extracellular domain (ECD) of human LRP6 and bound to non-overlapping epitopes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by epitope binning data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The LRP6 ECD contains four β-propeller motifs.
source: The LRP6 ECD contains four β-propeller motifs (Bao et al., 2012), and the N-terminal and C-terminal pairs interact with distinct classes of Wnt proteins represented by WNT1 or WNT3A (Bourhis et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2010), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao et al., 2012.

claim: The N-terminal and C-terminal pairs of β-propeller motifs in LRP6 interact with distinct classes of Wnt proteins represented by WNT1 or WNT3A, respectively.
source: The LRP6 ECD contains four β-propeller motifs (Bao et al., 2012), and the N-terminal and C-terminal pairs interact with distinct classes of Wnt proteins represented by WNT1 or WNT3A (Bourhis et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2010), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bourhis et al., 2010 and Gong et al., 2010.

claim: Ab L61 selectively inhibited βcatenin activation by WNT1.
source: Signaling assays revealed that Abs L61 and L63 selectively inhibited βcatenin activation by WNT1 or WNT3A, respectively (Figure 1B), suggesting that each Ab blocks one of the two distinct Wnt binding sites on LRP6.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ab L63 selectively inhibited βcatenin activation by WNT3A.
source: Signaling assays revealed that Abs L61 and L63 selectively inhibited βcatenin activation by WNT1 or WNT3A, respectively (Figure 1B), suggesting that each Ab blocks one of the two distinct Wnt binding sites on LRP6.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each Ab (L61 and L63) blocks one of the two distinct Wnt binding sites on LRP6.
source: Signaling assays revealed that Abs L61 and L63 selectively inhibited βcatenin activation by WNT1 or WNT3A, respectively (Figure 1B), suggesting that each Ab blocks one of the two distinct Wnt binding sites on LRP6.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective inhibition data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bispecific IgGs and diabody-Fc fusions using pan-FZD Ab FP and anti-LRP6 Abs L61 and L63 failed to activate βcatenin signaling and acted as Wnt signaling antagonists.
source: None of these Abs were able to activate βcatenin signaling, but rather, they all acted as Wnt signaling antagonists (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Bivalent recruitment of FZD/LRP6 heterodimers by bispecific Abs failed to recapitulate the stoichiometric, geometric or conformational properties of FZD/LRP6 complexes induced by natural Wnt ligands to stimulate signaling.
source: We thus concluded that bivalent recruitment of FZD/LRP6 heterodimers by bispecific Abs, using these configurations, failed to recapitulate the stoichiometric, geometric or conformational properties of FZD/LRP6 complexes induced by natural Wnt ligands to stimulate signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing lack of agonist activity.

claim: Wnt induces dimerization of FZD CRD.
source: Recent reports showed that Wnt induces dimerization of FZD CRD (Hirai et al., 2019; Nile et al., 2017) and that FZD and LRP6 clustering may be required for signaling (Carron et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2010; Hua et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hirai et al., 2019 and Nile et al., 2017.

claim: FZD and LRP6 clustering may be required for signaling.
source: Recent reports showed that Wnt induces dimerization of FZD CRD (Hirai et al., 2019; Nile et al., 2017) and that FZD and LRP6 clustering may be required for signaling (Carron et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2010; Hua et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carron et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2010; and Hua et al., 2018.

claim: FP+P-L63+3 and FP+P-L61+1 both activated βcatenin signaling but FP+P-L63+3 was ~10 fold more efficacious.
source: FP+P-L63+3 and FP+P-L61+1 both activated βcatenin signaling but the former was ~10 fold more efficacious (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FP+P-L61+3 was ~2 fold more efficacious than FP+P-L63+3.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, FP+P-L61+3 was~2 fold more efficacious than even FP+P-L63+3, indicating that engagement of a strong WNT3A site and a weak WNT1 site together is more effective than engagement of two strong WNT3A sites.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Engagement of a strong WNT3A site and a weak WNT1 site together is more effective than engagement of two strong WNT3A sites.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, FP+P-L61+3 was~2 fold more efficacious than even FP+P-L63+3, indicating that engagement of a strong WNT3A site and a weak WNT1 site together is more effective than engagement of two strong WNT3A sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative efficacy data.

claim: The two best FLAgs had single-digit nanomolar potency (EC50 ~5 nM).
source: The two best FLAgs had single-digit nanomolar potency (EC50 ~5 nM), which was virtually identical to the potency of purified WNT3A, and displayed a bell-shaped dose response profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: The potency of the best FLAgs was virtually identical to the potency of purified WNT3A.
source: The two best FLAgs had single-digit nanomolar potency (EC50 ~5 nM), which was virtually identical to the potency of purified WNT3A, and displayed a bell-shaped dose response profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is supported by comparative dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: The best FLAgs displayed a bell-shaped dose response profile.
source: The two best FLAgs had single-digit nanomolar potency (EC50 ~5 nM), which was virtually identical to the potency of purified WNT3A, and displayed a bell-shaped dose response profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is observed in the dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: Maximal stimulation by FLAgs requires multivalent binding.
source: We interpret this as indicating that maximal stimulation requires multivalent binding of the FLAg and that decreased efficacy at higher concentrations is likely attributable to monovalent binding to either FZD or LRP6.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bell-shaped dose-response curve.

claim: Decreased efficacy at higher FLAg concentrations is likely attributable to monovalent binding to either FZD or LRP6.
source: We interpret this as indicating that maximal stimulation requires multivalent binding of the FLAg and that decreased efficacy at higher concentrations is likely attributable to monovalent binding to either FZD or LRP6.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the bell-shaped dose-response curve.

claim: Treatment of RKO cells with FP+P-L61+3 caused dose- and time-dependent increases in βcatenin protein levels.
source: Treatment of RKO cells, which express low levels of βcatenin (Major et al., 2007), with FP+P-L61+3 caused dose- and time-dependent increases in βcatenin protein levels and phosphorylation of DVL2, a hallmark of Wnt-FZD pathway activation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Treatment of RKO cells with FP+P-L61+3 caused dose- and time-dependent increases in phosphorylation of DVL2.
source: Treatment of RKO cells, which express low levels of βcatenin (Major et al., 2007), with FP+P-L61+3 caused dose- and time-dependent increases in βcatenin protein levels and phosphorylation of DVL2, a hallmark of Wnt-FZD pathway activation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Phosphorylation of DVL2 is a hallmark of Wnt-FZD pathway activation.
source: Treatment of RKO cells, which express low levels of βcatenin (Major et al., 2007), with FP+P-L61+3 caused dose- and time-dependent increases in βcatenin protein levels and phosphorylation of DVL2, a hallmark of Wnt-FZD pathway activation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wnt signaling.

claim: RKO cells express low levels of βcatenin.
source: Treatment of RKO cells, which express low levels of βcatenin (Major et al., 2007), with FP+P-L61+3 caused dose- and time-dependent increases in βcatenin protein levels and phosphorylation of DVL2, a hallmark of Wnt-FZD pathway activation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Major et al., 2007.

claim: FLAg FP+P-L61+3 bound with affinities in the picomolar range (KD = 10–800 pM) to six FZDs (FZD1/2/4/5/7/8).
source: As anticipated, the FLAg bound with affinities in the picomolar range (KD = 10–800 pM) to the six FZDs recognized by the FZD diabodies derived from the parent pan-FZD paratope (Figure 1A) (Pavlovic et al., 2018) but did not bind detectably to the other three FZDs.
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FLAg FP+P-L61+3 did not bind detectably to FZD3, FZD6, FZD9, or FZD10.
source: As anticipated, the FLAg bound with affinities in the picomolar range (KD = 10–800 pM) to the six FZDs recognized by the FZD diabodies derived from the parent pan-FZD paratope (Figure 1A) (Pavlovic et al., 2018) but did not bind detectably to the other three FZDs.
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FLAg FP+P-L61+3 bound to LRP6 with affinity in the nanomolar range (KD = 12 nM).
source: Moreover, affinity for LRP6 was in the nanomolar range (KD = 12 nM).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The FLAg interacted with FcRn in a dose and pH dependent manner.
source: The FLAg behaved similarly to a conventional IgG and interacted with FcRn in a dose and pH dependent manner (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Natural IgGs bind to FcRn at pH 6.0 but not at pH 7.4, which enables recycling during pinocytosis and consequent long half-life in vivo.
source: Natural IgGs bind to FcRn at pH 6.0 but not at pH 7.4, and this enables recycling during pinocytosis and consequent long half-life in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibody pharmacokinetics.

claim: The FLAg behaved similarly to conventional IgG for interaction with Fc effectors including complement (C1q), CD16a, CD32a, and CD64.
source: The FLAg also behaved similarly to the IgG for interaction with other Fc effectors including complement (C1q), the natural killer cell marker CD16a, the B cell marker CD32a, and the monocyte and macrophage marker CD64 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The FLAg contains a functional Fc moiety that should confer effector functions and long half-life in vivo.
source: We conclude that the FLAg contains a functional Fc moiety that should confer effector functions and long half-life in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the FcRn and Fc effector binding data.

claim: Maximal stimulation by FP+P-L61+3 was reduced significantly by disabling one anti-FZD paratope.
source: βcatenin signaling assays showed that maximal stimulation was reduced significantly by disabling one anti-FZD paratope or the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT1 binding site and was completely ablated by disabling the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT3A binding site or by simultaneously disabling one anti-FZD paratope and either of the anti-LRP6 paratopes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Maximal stimulation by FP+P-L61+3 was reduced significantly by disabling the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT1 binding site.
source: βcatenin signaling assays showed that maximal stimulation was reduced significantly by disabling one anti-FZD paratope or the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT1 binding site and was completely ablated by disabling the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT3A binding site or by simultaneously disabling one anti-FZD paratope and either of the anti-LRP6 paratopes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Maximal stimulation by FP+P-L61+3 was completely ablated by disabling the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT3A binding site.
source: βcatenin signaling assays showed that maximal stimulation was reduced significantly by disabling one anti-FZD paratope or the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT1 binding site and was completely ablated by disabling the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT3A binding site or by simultaneously disabling one anti-FZD paratope and either of the anti-LRP6 paratopes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Maximal stimulation by FP+P-L61+3 was completely ablated by simultaneously disabling one anti-FZD paratope and either of the anti-LRP6 paratopes.
source: βcatenin signaling assays showed that maximal stimulation was reduced significantly by disabling one anti-FZD paratope or the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT1 binding site and was completely ablated by disabling the anti-LRP6 paratope for the WNT3A binding site or by simultaneously disabling one anti-FZD paratope and either of the anti-LRP6 paratopes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FP+P-L5/63 exhibited activity similar to FP+P-L61+3 (EC50 = 4 nM).
source: We also substituted an anti-LRP5 paratope targeting the WNT3A binding site for the anti-LRP6 paratope targeting the WNT1 binding site to generate a molecule (FP+P-L5/63) that could recruit both co-receptors and observed activity similar to that of FP+P-L61+3 (Figure 2D, EC50 = 4 nM).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Optimal agonist activity is achieved with a molecule capable of recruiting two FZDs through a common epitope and LRP6 through two distinct epitopes.
source: Taken together, these data showed that optimal agonist activity is achieved with a molecule capable of recruiting two FZDs through a common epitope and LRP6 through two distinct epitopes, but activity can be modulated to intermediate levels by disabling one of the anti-FZD or anti-LRP6 paratopes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paratope dissection experiments.

claim: FLAg activity can be modulated to intermediate levels by disabling one of the anti-FZD or anti-LRP6 paratopes.
source: Taken together, these data showed that optimal agonist activity is achieved with a molecule capable of recruiting two FZDs through a common epitope and LRP6 through two distinct epitopes, but activity can be modulated to intermediate levels by disabling one of the anti-FZD or anti-LRP6 paratopes.
evidence: This is supported by the paratope dissection data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: FP*+P*-L61+3 (with anti-FZD scFvs) exhibited activity similar to FP+P-L61+3.
source: Compared with FP+P-L61+3, a FLAg that contained anti-FZD scFvs (FP*+P*-L61+3) exhibited similar activity, whereas activity was significantly reduced for FLAgs that contained anti-LRP6 scFvs (FP+P-L61*+3*) or scFvs at both ends (FP*+P*-L61*+3*).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Activity was significantly reduced for FLAgs that contained anti-LRP6 scFvs (FP+P-L61*+3*).
source: Compared with FP+P-L61+3, a FLAg that contained anti-FZD scFvs (FP*+P*-L61+3) exhibited similar activity, whereas activity was significantly reduced for FLAgs that contained anti-LRP6 scFvs (FP+P-L61*+3*) or scFvs at both ends (FP*+P*-L61*+3*).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Activity was significantly reduced for FLAgs with scFvs at both ends (FP*+P*-L61*+3*).
source: Compared with FP+P-L61+3, a FLAg that contained anti-FZD scFvs (FP*+P*-L61+3) exhibited similar activity, whereas activity was significantly reduced for FLAgs that contained anti-LRP6 scFvs (FP+P-L61*+3*) or scFvs at both ends (FP*+P*-L61*+3*).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Differences in activity between diabody and scFv formats were not due to differences in affinity.
source: These differences in activity were not due to differences in affinity, as BLI measurements showed comparable, high-affinity binding to LRP6 and FZD isoforms regardless of whether paratopes were presented in the diabody or scFv format (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by BLI binding data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: Particular stoichiometries and geometries are required for the assembly of optimal FZD/LRP6 signaling complexes.
source: Taken together, these results showed that particular stoichiometries and geometries are required for the assembly of optimal FZD/LRP6 signaling complexes, and constraints are especially precise for LRP6, which requires engagement of two distinct epitopes in a specific geometry dictated by the diabody format.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of diabody and scFv formats.

claim: Constraints are especially precise for LRP6, which requires engagement of two distinct epitopes in a specific geometry dictated by the diabody format.
source: Taken together, these results showed that particular stoichiometries and geometries are required for the assembly of optimal FZD/LRP6 signaling complexes, and constraints are especially precise for LRP6, which requires engagement of two distinct epitopes in a specific geometry dictated by the diabody format.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced activity of scFv-containing FLAgs targeting LRP6.

claim: Looser constraints for FZD engagement enabled significant activation with a single anti-FZD paratope.
source: Notably, the looser constraints for FZD engagement enabled significant activation with a single anti-FZD paratope (Figure 2C), which opens the door for further enhancing specificity or altering signaling by recruiting a different cell surface protein through an additional paratope in conjunction with an anti-FZD paratope at the N-termini of the heterodimeric Fc.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A FLAg containing two identical anti-FZD5 paratopes exhibited monospecificity for FZD5.
source: A FLAg containing two identical anti-FZD5 paratopes exhibited monospecificity for FZD5.
evidence: This is supported by specificity data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When paired with one of the other monospecific anti-FZD paratopes, the anti-FZD5 paratope acted in an additive manner, enabling the facile assembly of bispecific FLAgs in a predictable manner.
source: Moreover, when paired with one of the other monospecific anti-FZD paratopes, the anti-FZD5 paratope acted in an additive manner, enabling the facile assembly of bispecific FLAgs in a predictable manner (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by specificity data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bispecific FLAgs maintain high affinities for the respective targeted Frizzled.
source: Importantly, bispecific FLAgs maintain high affinities for the respective targeted Frizzled (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C).
evidence: This is supported by binding data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Each Wnt protein may be endowed with a particular function determined by its FZD specificity profile.
source: Recent genetic and functional data support the idea that each Wnt protein may be endowed with a particular function determined by its FZD specificity profile (Dijksterhuis et al., 2015; Voloshanenko et al., 2017), and thus, FLAgs that mimic the specificities of particular Wnts would be useful analogs of those Wnt isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dijksterhuis et al., 2015 and Voloshanenko et al., 2017.

claim: Treatment of RNF43 mutant pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line HPAF-II with LGK974 led to cell cycle arrest and potent inhibition of proliferation.
source: Treatment of RNF43 mutant pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line HPAF-II with LGK974, a small molecule that inhibits all Wnt secretion, led to cell cycle arrest and potent inhibition of proliferation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cell proliferation of HPAF-II cells was partially rescued by WNT3A conditioned media.
source: Cell proliferation was partially rescued by WNT3A conditioned media and was fully rescued by a pan-FZD or FZD5-specific FLAg, which is consistent with these cells requiring signaling through FZD5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cell proliferation of HPAF-II cells was fully rescued by a pan-FZD or FZD5-specific FLAg.
source: Cell proliferation was partially rescued by WNT3A conditioned media and was fully rescued by a pan-FZD or FZD5-specific FLAg, which is consistent with these cells requiring signaling through FZD5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HPAF-II cells require signaling through FZD5.
source: Cell proliferation was partially rescued by WNT3A conditioned media and was fully rescued by a pan-FZD or FZD5-specific FLAg, which is consistent with these cells requiring signaling through FZD5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue data and is consistent with prior genetic data.

claim: FZDs 1, 2 and 7 are required for Wnt-mediated βcatenin activation in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with genetic data (Voloshanenko et al., 2017) showing that FZDs 1, 2 and 7 are required for Wnt-mediated βcatenin activation in HEK293 cells, FLAgs specific for FZD2 or FZD7 activated βcatenin robustly in these cells whereas FLAgs specific for FZD4 or FZD5 did not (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Voloshanenko et al., 2017.

claim: FLAgs specific for FZD2 or FZD7 activated βcatenin robustly in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with genetic data (Voloshanenko et al., 2017) showing that FZDs 1, 2 and 7 are required for Wnt-mediated βcatenin activation in HEK293 cells, FLAgs specific for FZD2 or FZD7 activated βcatenin robustly in these cells whereas FLAgs specific for FZD4 or FZD5 did not (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: FLAgs specific for FZD4 or FZD5 did not activate βcatenin in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with genetic data (Voloshanenko et al., 2017) showing that FZDs 1, 2 and 7 are required for Wnt-mediated βcatenin activation in HEK293 cells, FLAgs specific for FZD2 or FZD7 activated βcatenin robustly in these cells whereas FLAgs specific for FZD4 or FZD5 did not (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by signaling assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Modulation of Wnt-βcatenin signaling activity is integral to most PSCs differentiation protocols.
source: Modulation of Wnt-βcatenin signaling activity is integral to most PSCs differentiation protocols (Huggins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huggins et al., 2016.

claim: Treatment of human PSCs with WNT3A conditioned media or small molecule inhibitors of GSK3 activates βcatenin signaling, leads to primitive streak induction, and promotes mesodermal fate specification.
source: Treatment of human PSCs with WNT3A conditioned media, or small molecule inhibitors of GSK3, activates βcatenin signaling, leads to primitive streak induction, and promotes mesodermal fate specification (Davidson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davidson et al., 2012.

claim: Treatment with 30 nM FP+P-L61+3 for three days caused robust induction of the mesoderm marker BRACHYURY and decreased expression of the pluripotency marker OCT4 to levels comparable to treatment with the GSK3 inhibitor CHIR99021 at 6 μM.
source: We evaluated FLAg activity in this context and found that treatment with 30 nM FP+P-L61+3 for three days caused robust induction of the mesoderm marker BRACHYURY and decreased expression of the pluripotency marker OCT4 to levels comparable to treatment with the GSK3 inhibitor CHIR99021 at 6 μM (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Wnt proteins secreted by paneth cells are sufficient to support the growth of mouse small intestine organoids in the presence of R-spondins.
source: In vitro, Wnt proteins secreted by paneth cells are sufficient to support the growth of mouse small intestine organoids in the presence of R-spondins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about intestinal organoid culture.

claim: Addition of either WNT3A conditioned media or FP+P-L61+3 completely rescued the growth defects of mouse small intestine organoids caused by LGK974.
source: To assess whether a FLAg could substitute for endogenous Wnts, we treated the organoids with LGK974, which ablated Wnt production and inhibited growth completely, and asked whether FP+P-L61+3 could rescue growth. Addition of either WNT3A conditioned media or FP+P-L61+3 completely rescued the growth defects caused by LGK974 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by organoid viability data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Human colorectal organoids do not have paneth cells and thus require exogenous source of Wnt growth factors.
source: Contrary to mouse small intestine organoids, human colorectal organoids do not have paneth cells and thus require exogenous source of Wnt growth factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human colorectal organoid culture.

claim: Incorporation of WNT3A conditioned media or FP+P-L61+3 was sufficient to propagate human colorectal organoids for multiple passages.
source: Incorporation of WNT3A conditioned media or FP+P-L61+3 was sufficient to propagate these organoids for multiple passages (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by organoid culture and viability data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: A pan-FZD FLAg can substitute for Wnt proteins to support growth of tissue organoids.
source: We conclude that a pan-FZD FLAg can substitute for Wnt proteins to support growth of tissue organoids, and thus, the FLAg is a defined component that could alleviate limitations associated with the use of conditioned media or purified Wnt proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the organoid rescue experiments.

claim: FP+P-L61+3 recognizes mouse FZDs and LRP6.
source: FP+P-L61+3 recognizes mouse FZDs and LRP6, and it contains an Fc that interacts with the FcRn and should endow it with a long, Ab-like, half-life in vivo.
evidence: This is implied by the successful in vivo experiments in mice.

claim: FP+P-L61+3 contains an Fc that interacts with the FcRn and should endow it with a long, Ab-like, half-life in vivo.
source: FP+P-L61+3 recognizes mouse FZDs and LRP6, and it contains an Fc that interacts with the FcRn and should endow it with a long, Ab-like, half-life in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the FcRn binding data and general knowledge of antibody pharmacokinetics.

claim: Within the intestinal stem cell niche, Wnt proteins secreted by mesenchymal cells induce expression of βcatenin target genes in stem cells at the bottom of the crypt to direct their self-renewal.
source: Within the intestinal stem cell niche, Wnt proteins secreted by mesenchymal cells induce expression of βcatenin target genes in stem cells at the bottom of the crypt to direct their self-renewal, and the target gene LGR5 is frequently used as a marker of stem cells in various tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about intestinal stem cell biology.

claim: LGR5 is frequently used as a marker of stem cells in various tissues.
source: Within the intestinal stem cell niche, Wnt proteins secreted by mesenchymal cells induce expression of βcatenin target genes in stem cells at the bottom of the crypt to direct their self-renewal, and the target gene LGR5 is frequently used as a marker of stem cells in various tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge in stem cell biology.

claim: Treatment of LGR5-GFP mice with C59 ablated Wnt production and caused rapid extinction of LGR5 expression and the linked GFP signal in crypt stem cells.
source: Treatment of LGR5-GFP mice with C59 ablated Wnt production and caused rapid extinction of LGR5 expression and the linked GFP signal in crypt stem cells.
evidence: This is supported by the in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: GFP expression in LGR5-GFP mice was rescued upon co-treatment with FP+P-L61+3 by intraperitoneal injection.
source: Strikingly, GFP expression was rescued upon co-treatment with FP+P-L61+3 by intraperitoneal injection (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: FP+P-L61+3 has a sufficient half-life and bioavailability to enable βcatenin activation at levels that promote self-renewal of intestinal stem cells in the absence of endogenous Wnt.
source: We conclude that FP+P-L61+3 has a sufficient half-life and bioavailability to enable βcatenin activation at levels that promote self-renewal of intestinal stem cells in the absence of endogenous Wnt.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo rescue experiments.

claim: The requirement for tetravalency in optimal FLAgs likely indicates that maximal activity requires assembly of FZD and LRP5/6 in higher order complexes.
source: In terms of mechanism of action, the requirement for tetravalency in optimal FLAgs likely indicates that maximal activity requires assembly of FZD and LRP5/6 in higher order complexes.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The fact that FP+P-L61+3 was more active than FP+P-L63+3 suggests that engagement of both Wnt binding sites within LRP6 may result in intramolecular rearrangements that stabilize conformations that are more favorable for signaling activity.
source: Also, the fact that FP+P-L61+3 was more active than FP+P-L63+3 suggests that engagement of both Wnt binding sites within LRP6 may result in intramolecular rearrangements that stabilize conformations that are more favorable for signaling activity.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation of the comparative activity data.

claim: Recent structural work reported a 2:2 stoichiometry of Wnt ligand and FZD CRD that could be modeled to recruit two LRP5/6 molecules.
source: Intriguingly, recent structural work reported a 2:2 stoichiometry of Wnt ligand and FZD CRD that could be modeled to recruit two LRP5/6 molecules (Hirai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hirai et al., 2019.

claim: Bivalent recruitment of one FZD and one LRP5/6 molecule is sufficient for signaling activity but engagement of an oligomeric complex, composed of two FZD and one or two LRP5/6 molecules, is required for maximal activation.
source: Our results suggest that bivalent recruitment of one FZD and one LRP5/6 molecule is sufficient for signaling activity but engagement of an oligomeric complex, composed of two FZD and one or two LRP5/6 molecules, is required for maximal activation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Tetravalent FLAg molecules may be better than bivalent agonists for recapitulating mechanisms employed by Wnt proteins to engage FZD-LRP5/6 receptor complexes.
source: Therefore, tetravalent FLAg molecules may be better than bivalent agonists for recapitulating mechanisms employed by Wnt proteins to engage FZD-LRP5/6 receptor complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the comparative activity data.
